abstract: ArXiv:2606.00962v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Foundational agent interoperability standards, notably the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol and the Model Context Protocol (MCP), have advanced multi-agent system communication, and complementary identity frameworks leveraging W3C Decentralised Identifiers (DIDs) and Verifiable Credentials (VCs) provide cryptographic agent authentication. However, no existing protocol supports content-based semantic routing of agent payloads across organisational trust boundaries without requiring the routing intermediary to decrypt the payload, which is a hard constraint in compliance-sensitive environments governed by GDPR, HIPAA, and MiFID II. We propose SS-ZKR, a three-mechanism privacy-preserving routing protocol designed as a complementary layer atop A2A/MCP. Mechanism I introduces blind routing via differentially private semantic intent vectors cryptographically bound to zero-knowledge proofs of payload-schema consistency. Mechanism II offers vector-weighted adaptive payload sanitisation with formal (epsilon, delta)-differential privacy for numerical fields and heuristic semantic aggregation for textual fields. Mechanism III presents a spatial-to-cryptographic policy compiler that translates visually defined trust-zone topologies into deterministic zero-knowledge access circuits. We provide a formal threat model, analyse information leakage bounds of intent vectors, present pseudocode for all three mechanisms, and give analytical complexity comparisons against TEE-based and homomorphic encryption-based routing baselines. SS-ZKR lets enterprises in financial services, healthcare, and defence orchestrate heterogeneous AI agents across regulatory boundaries without exposing proprietary data to routing infrastructure.
tldr: SS-ZKR is a privacy-preserving routing protocol for multi-agent systems that uses differential privacy and zero-knowledge proofs to enable semantic routing without decrypting payloads.
motivation: Existing agent communication protocols lack privacy-preserving content-based routing across trust boundaries, which is required for compliance with regulations like GDPR and HIPAA.
method: The protocol combines blind routing with differentially private intent vectors and zero-knowledge proofs, adaptive payload sanitization with differential privacy, and a spatial-to-cryptographic policy compiler.
result: The paper provides formal threat models, information leakage bounds, pseudocode, and complexity comparisons against TEE-based and homomorphic encryption baselines.
conclusion: SS-ZKR enables secure multi-agent collaboration in regulated industries, but its relevance to quantum information science is minimal.

title: How (and When) Can You Fit Examples To Logic-based Hypothesis Classes Over Infinite Structures?
authors: Alessio Mansutti Michael Benedikt
abstract: ArXiv:2606.01107v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study fitting problems, sometimes called ``training problems'', where we have a finite sample consisting of inputs and outputs, and we want to know whether there is a function in a certain class that could produce these outputs, exactly or approximately, on the given inputs. We focus on the computational and descriptive complexity of fitting for logically-defined classes in common decidable structures, like the real ordered field and Presburger arithmetic, and also for broader classes defined via combinatorial or model-theoretic properties. We isolate the complexity of these fitting problems, with particular attention to cases where we can use queries in a natural query language over the sample to determine whether a sample is fittable.
tldr: This paper studies the computational complexity of fitting examples to logic-based hypothesis classes over infinite structures, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To understand the descriptive and computational complexity of fitting problems for logically-defined classes in decidable structures like real ordered fields and Presburger arithmetic.
method: The authors analyze fitting problems using tools from computational complexity and model theory, focusing on query languages over finite samples.
result: They isolate the complexity of fitting problems for various logical classes, identifying cases where natural query languages can determine fittability.
conclusion: The work provides a complexity-theoretic classification of fitting problems, with implications for learning theory and database theory, but not for quantum information.

title: On The Complexity Of Recurrence Evaluation
authors: Michael Vyalyi Artem Parfenov
abstract: ArXiv:2606.01175v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we study the complexity of the recurrence evaluation problem. We are interested in finitely valued recurrent functions. We present two results in this direction. First, we study the recurrence problem for sequences, assuming that a recurrence relation is defined by a fixed function, while the offsets are part of the input. Depending on the form of presentation (whether the offsets are given in unary or in binary), the problem is PSPACE-complete or EXP-complete. Second, we study recurrences defined by the NAND function. They are related to impartial games. We prove PP-hardness of the recurrence evaluation problem for a very simple 3-dimensional game, in which the offset vectors are coordinate vectors (1,0,0), (0,1,0) and (0,0,1) but the boundary conditions are arbitrary. In other words, we consider generalized winning conditions for the game extending the normal and the mis\`ere winning conditions.
tldr: This paper studies the computational complexity of evaluating finitely valued recurrent functions, showing PSPACE-completeness and EXP-completeness for different offset encodings, and PP-hardness for a 3D impartial game with NAND recurrences.
motivation: To understand the inherent difficulty of evaluating recurrence relations, which appear in many areas of computer science and mathematics.
method: The authors use complexity theory reductions, analyzing the impact of offset encoding (unary vs binary) and specific recurrence functions like NAND.
result: The recurrence evaluation problem is PSPACE-complete when offsets are given in unary and EXP-complete when given in binary. For NAND-based recurrences related to impartial games, the problem is PP-hard even for a simple 3D game with unit coordinate vectors.
conclusion: The results establish tight complexity bounds for recurrence evaluation, highlighting the role of input encoding and the hardness of certain game-theoretic recurrences.

title: Modulation-Reaction Networks
authors: Yo\`av Montacute Leo Lobski
abstract: ArXiv:2606.01193v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Biochemical systems involve both the flow of matter, in which entities transform into one another via reactions, and the flow of information, in which entities regulate which reactions may occur. Boolean networks capture the latter; reaction networks capture the former. Yet no unified qualitative formalism treats regulated reactions as its principal objects of study, despite their prominence in standards such as the Systems Biology Graphical Notation Process Description (SBGN-PD) language. We introduce modulation-reaction networks (MR-networks), a mathematical framework in which entities modulate reactions through activations and inhibitions, and study their synchronous Boolean semantics. To reason about MR-networks we develop Modulation-Reaction Logic (MRL), a hybrid modal [MATH]-calculus whose modalities reason about the structure of the network and whose fixed-point operators capture temporal evolution of the computation. We establish a collection of validities, including a complete characterisation of the one-step update rule, and demonstrate the expressive power of MRL by formalising properties of biological interest such as reachability, sustained production, and presence of attractors. We show that MRL admits model-checking via an evaluation game, and introduce a bisimulation relation for MR-networks, which is proved to be invariant for all MRL-formulas. As a step towards a biologically more realistic computational model, we sketch the asynchronous semantics of MR-networks, and outline how the developments for the synchronous case transfer to the study of the asynchronous one.
tldr: The paper introduces modulation-reaction networks (MR-networks) as a unified formalism for biochemical systems with regulation, and develops a modal μ-calculus logic (MRL) for reasoning about their synchronous Boolean semantics.
motivation: Existing formalisms (Boolean networks, reaction networks) treat either information flow or matter flow, but not both in a unified way. The authors aim to provide a mathematical framework that captures regulated reactions as primary objects, as seen in standards like SBGN-PD.
method: The paper defines MR-networks mathematically, develops Modulation-Reaction Logic (MRL) as a hybrid modal μ-calculus, establishes validities including a complete characterization of the one-step update rule, and introduces a bisimulation relation. It also sketches asynchronous semantics.
result: MRL can express biologically relevant properties (reachability, sustained production, attractors) and admits model-checking via an evaluation game. The bisimulation is invariant for all MRL formulas.
conclusion: The framework provides a foundation for analyzing regulated biochemical networks, with potential extensions to asynchronous dynamics and more realistic models.

title: Cooperative Mitigation Against Learning-Based Reactive Jammers: Analysis And Sdr Validation
authors: J. Harshan Soumita Hazra
abstract: ArXiv:2606.01197v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Motivated by recent developments in full-duplex radios, cognitive radios, and data-driven signal-processing, we propose a novel class of reactive jamming adversaries wherein the adversary transmits jamming energy on the victim's frequency band while simultaneously monitoring various energy statistics in the network to detect the presence of potential countermeasures, thereby trapping the victim. These adversaries employ generalized energy detectors comprising statistical detectors, based on instantaneous and distributional energy metrics, and data-driven detectors employing machine-learning classifiers to learn patterns in the observed energy sequences. Against such a strong adversary, we propose a family of cooperative mitigation strategies wherein the victim takes assistance from a helper node, with the strategies tailored to operate under a wide range of latency requirements on victim's messages and practical radio hardware constraints at helper node. To provide theoretical guarantees on their efficacy, interesting optimization problems are formulated on the choice of their underlying parameters, followed by extensive mathematical analyses on their error performance and covertness. To assess their practical feasibility, we implement the before-deployment and after-deployment setups on a software-defined-radio-based hardware testbed, and to evaluate their detectability on real energy observations, we collect the corresponding datasets to train and test the data-driven machine-learning classifiers employed by adversary. Both analytical and hardware evaluations show that the proposed strategies cannot be detected with a high-probability under the generalized energy detectors used by adversary.
tldr: This paper proposes cooperative mitigation strategies against learning-based reactive jammers in wireless networks, with theoretical analysis and SDR validation.
motivation: To counter advanced reactive jamming adversaries that use machine learning to detect countermeasures, ensuring reliable communication.
method: The authors design cooperative strategies with a helper node, formulate optimization problems for parameter selection, and implement the system on an SDR testbed with real energy datasets.
result: Both analytical and hardware evaluations show the proposed strategies achieve high undetectability against generalized energy detectors including ML-based classifiers.
conclusion: The work demonstrates practical feasibility of cooperative jamming mitigation, but is focused on wireless security rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Verifiable Criteria And Properties For Interval $B_{\pi}^{R^I}$-Tensors
authors: Yisheng Song Li Ye
abstract: ArXiv:2606.00475v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper introduces interval [MATH]-tensors as a natural extension of [MATH]-tensors to the interval setting. We provide two practical verifiable criteria for an interval tensor to be an interval [MATH]-tensor, one based on endpoint inequalities and another constructing an explicit vector [MATH]. Connections with interval [MATH]-tensors, positive definite interval tensors, and interval [MATH]-tensors are established. Applications in polynomial optimization and interval tensor complementarity problems are briefly discussed.
tldr: This paper introduces interval BπR^I-tensors, a mathematical extension of B-tensors to interval settings, with verifiable criteria and applications in polynomial optimization and complementarity problems.
motivation: To extend the concept of B-tensors to interval tensors, providing practical criteria for identification and exploring connections with other tensor classes.
method: The authors define interval BπR^I-tensors and provide two verifiable criteria: one based on endpoint inequalities and another constructing an explicit vector. They also establish relationships with interval B-tensors, positive definite interval tensors, and interval M-tensors.
result: Two practical verifiable criteria for an interval tensor to be an interval BπR^I-tensor are given, along with connections to other tensor types. Applications in polynomial optimization and interval tensor complementarity problems are briefly discussed.
conclusion: The work contributes to the theory of interval tensors, with potential applications in optimization and complementarity problems, but further research is needed to explore practical implementations.

title: A Path-following Framework On Fiber Bundle For Variational Inequalities
authors: Hongbo Sun
abstract: ArXiv:2606.00778v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Variational inequality (VI) is a fundamental mathematical framework for many classical problems. We present a path-following framework for finite-dimensional VIs with arbitrary continuous functions and compact convex domains. The approach first approximately reduces a general VI to a smooth VI on simplex. Its key innovation is to formulate the smooth VI on simplex on a fiber bundle called the fixed-point bundle. Exploiting this geometric structure, we systematically integrate starting point selection, path-following, and singularity avoidance. Without any assumptions such as monotonicity, the algorithm guarantees global linear convergence to nonsingular solutions. For singular solutions, it retains global linear reduction up to a fixed precision, after which convergence becomes sublinear as the required precision increases. In numerical experiments on 14400 randomly generated VIs of up to 800 dimensions, the algorithm succeeds in every instance, and iteration number increases only mildly with the dimension.
tldr: A path-following framework for solving variational inequalities using fiber bundle geometry, with global convergence guarantees.
motivation: To develop a robust algorithm for finite-dimensional variational inequalities that does not require monotonicity or other restrictive assumptions.
method: Reduces a general VI to a smooth VI on a simplex, then formulates it on a fiber bundle (fixed-point bundle) to integrate starting point selection, path-following, and singularity avoidance.
result: The algorithm guarantees global linear convergence to nonsingular solutions and sublinear convergence near singular solutions; numerical experiments on 14400 random VIs up to 800 dimensions show 100% success with mild iteration growth.
conclusion: Provides a geometrically motivated, provably convergent method for VIs, with potential extensions to infinite-dimensional or stochastic settings.

title: Coupled Routing And Charge Schedule Optimization Of Electrified Delivery Truck Fleets: Feasibility Analyses
authors: Yared Tadesse Wendimagegnehu, Beshah Ayalew, Andrej Ivanco, Habtamu Hailemichael
abstract: ArXiv:2606.00792v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Electrifying truck fleets has the potential to improve energy efficiency and reduce carbon emissions from the freight transportation sector. However, the range limitations and substantial capital costs with current battery technologies imposes constraints that challenge the overall cost feasibility of electrifying fleets for logistics companies. In this paper, we investigate the coupled routing and charge scheduling optimization of a delivery fleet serving a large urban area as one approach to discovering feasible pathways. To this end, we first build an improved energy consumption model for a Class 7-8 electric and diesel truck using a data-driven approach of generating energy consumption data from detailed powertrain simulations on numerous drive cycles. We then conduct several analyses on the impact of battery pack capacity, cost, and electricity prices on the amortized daily total cost of fleet electrification at different penetration levels, considering availability of fast charging at the depot. Findings indicate that at typical energy density of current battery technology, there is an optimal battery pack capacity that results from the contradicting effects of increasing pack capacity on cost, life span, weight and energy consumption. It is also observed that with currently improving trends in battery pack costs and availability of reduced electricity prices at the depot, such as with renewable microgrids, fleet electrification can become viable even at low levels of penetration.
tldr: This paper optimizes routing and charging for electric delivery truck fleets to assess cost feasibility, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To evaluate the economic viability of electrifying truck fleets given current battery limitations and costs.
method: Builds an energy consumption model for Class 7-8 trucks using data-driven powertrain simulations, then analyzes battery capacity, cost, and electricity prices on total daily cost.
result: Finds an optimal battery pack capacity balancing cost, lifespan, weight, and energy consumption; fleet electrification can become viable with improving battery costs and cheap depot electricity.
conclusion: Fleet electrification is feasible under certain cost and infrastructure conditions, but the paper does not address quantum or thermodynamic aspects.

title: From Bungee To $c^1$ And $c^0$ Hamiltonian Systems And Their Integrability And Nonintegrability
authors: Vladimir Dragovi\'c, Borislav Gaji\'c, Bo\v{z}idar Jovanovi\'c
abstract: ArXiv:2606.00870v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider natural Hamiltonian systems with potentials that are [MATH] or [MATH] on a hypersurface and [MATH]-smooth in the complement and introduce and study corresponding notions of their integrabilty and non-integrability. As a motivating example, we derive and analyze models of bungee jumping. We provide prototype examples of the Liuoville-Arnol'd theorem for [MATH] and [MATH] Hamiltonians.
tldr: The paper studies integrability and non-integrability of Hamiltonian systems with low-regularity potentials, using bungee jumping as a motivating example.
motivation: To extend classical integrability theory to Hamiltonians that are only C^1 or C^0 on a hypersurface, motivated by realistic physical models like bungee jumping.
method: Analytical and geometric methods, including generalizations of the Liouville-Arnold theorem for non-smooth Hamiltonians.
result: Provides prototype examples and conditions for integrability/non-integrability of such systems.
conclusion: The work opens up study of integrability in low-regularity Hamiltonian systems, with potential applications in mechanics and control.

title: Tiny Recursive Models For Solving The J2-Perturbed Lambert Problem
authors: Roberto Armellin Minduli Wijayatunga
abstract: ArXiv:2606.00895v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents a fast, recursive neural solver for the J2-perturbed Lambert problem based on Tiny Recursive Models (TRM), termed the TRM-Perturbed Lambert (TRM-PL) model. TRM is a weight-shared architecture whose effective capacity emerges from iteration depth rather than parameter count: a compact reasoning module is applied repeatedly within a two-level latent hierarchy, refining a candidate departure velocity by simulating the J2 trajectory and correcting it from the resulting tracking error. This unifies initial-guess generation and iterative correction in a single, end-to-end differentiable architecture. The recursive refinement loop is a learned alternative to the homotopy and continuation schemes of classical perturbed-Lambert solvers: rather than following a hand-designed path from the Keplerian to the perturbed solution, the network learns its own sequence of corrections. We evaluate TRM-PL on three test cases of increasing difficulty: single-revolution low-Earth-orbit (LEO) transfers, multi-revolution LEO transfers, and multi-revolution Jovian transfers. Three training paradigms are compared: jointly learning the Lambert solution and the J2 correction; refining the Lambert initial velocity with target-position and J2-corrected velocity supervision; and refining it with target-position supervision alone. Across all cases, the refinement-only approaches are the most reliable. The position-supervised variant reduces the median terminal-position error from 21.7 km to 0.027 km on single-revolution LEO, from 340.9 km to 0.31 km on multi-revolution LEO, all with the same 2.3M-parameter architecture. A single Newton corrector iteration on the TRM-PL output tightens the Jovian median to 0.063 km, yielding compact models accurate enough for embedded deployment.
tldr: This paper presents a neural network solver for the J2-perturbed Lambert problem in astrodynamics, using recursive weight-shared architectures to refine initial guesses.
motivation: To develop a fast, accurate, and compact solver for the J2-perturbed Lambert problem, which is computationally intensive for classical methods, especially for embedded systems.
method: A Tiny Recursive Model (TRM) with a weight-shared reasoning module applied iteratively in a two-level latent hierarchy, trained end-to-end to refine departure velocities by simulating J2 trajectories and correcting errors.
result: The TRM-PL model achieves median terminal-position errors as low as 0.027 km on single-revolution LEO transfers and 0.31 km on multi-revolution LEO transfers with only 2.3M parameters, and a single Newton corrector iteration reduces Jovian errors to 0.063 km.
conclusion: The approach demonstrates that learned recursive refinement can replace classical homotopy methods, yielding compact models suitable for embedded deployment in astrodynamics.

title: On The History Of The Square And Multiply Algorithm
authors: Nuh Aydin, Mohammad K. Azarian, Omid Khormali, Ghaya Mtimet
abstract: ArXiv:2606.00958v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The square-and-multiply algorithm, also known as binary exponentiation or repeated squaring, is a technique for fast exponentiation commonly used in modern cryptography and computational number theory. Despite its prominence, the historical origins of the algorithm are not known with certainty. This paper critically examines the origins and formalization of the algorithm through primary source analysis. We focus on Jamshid al-Kashi's fifteenth-century Miftah al-Hisab where the algorithm is articulated explicitly as a general method and claimed by al-Kashi as his own innovation. To contextualize this, we trace earlier instances of successive squaring in the works of al-Uqlidisi and al-Biruni, who applied these techniques for specific calculations, but did not formalize them into a general procedure. The earliest known work on this method of computation is found in Pingala's prosodic studies in ancient India (c. 200 BCE). Even though it was not fully developed as a general technique, Pingala's work seems to contain the conceptual foundation of the algorithm which is to employ the binary representation of a positive integer. By mapping this intellectual progression, the paper illustrates the historical background of an algorithm that is prominent in modern computation.
tldr: This paper traces the historical development of the square-and-multiply algorithm from ancient Indian prosody to al-Kashi's formalization.
motivation: To clarify the uncertain historical origins of the square-and-multiply algorithm through primary source analysis.
method: Critical examination of historical texts including works by Pingala, al-Uqlidisi, al-Biruni, and al-Kashi.
result: The algorithm's conceptual foundation appears in Pingala's work (c. 200 BCE), with successive squaring used by later scholars, but al-Kashi first articulated it as a general method.
conclusion: The paper provides a historical narrative but does not present new technical results; it is primarily of historical interest.

title: How To Compare The Security Of Code Written By Humans To LLM-generated Code
authors: Jasmine Egl Rebecca Balebako
abstract: ArXiv:2606.00186v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly transforming how software is created and maintained. Comparing LLM-generated code against human-written standards is essential to determine whether these new tools uphold or erode the security baselines established by professional developers. Yet, we lack a standardized method for empirically comparing the security of code produced through human-LLM collaboration against LLM-only, or traditional human-only methods. To facilitate this, we propose an automated framework for conducting comparative studies across human-only, LLM-only, and hybrid conditions. Our approach automates the logging of prompts, timing, and experimental settings, measuring outcomes through multi-dimensional static and dynamic quality analysis. We provide an open-source implementation of this framework to ensure that future researchers can conduct reproducible, species-fair experiments. Importantly, we validate the framework via a feasibility study, providing an experimental blueprint for ``species-fair'' comparisons between human and AI subjects. By sharing lessons learned, we establish a foundation for empirical research on human and LLM-generated code for software security.
tldr: This paper proposes a framework for comparing the security of code written by humans, LLMs, and hybrid human-LLM collaboration, but is unrelated to quantum computing or information thermodynamics.
motivation: There is a lack of standardized methods to empirically compare the security of code produced by humans, LLMs, and hybrid approaches.
method: The authors develop an automated framework that logs prompts, timing, and settings, and uses multi-dimensional static and dynamic quality analysis to measure outcomes.
result: The framework is validated via a feasibility study, providing a blueprint for 'species-fair' comparisons between human and AI code generation.
conclusion: The work establishes a foundation for empirical research on human and LLM-generated code security, but does not address quantum computing or related topics.

title: Beyond Edge Coverage: Per-Task Data-Flow Extraction At Kernel Function Boundaries Via Llvm
authors: Yunseong Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2606.00455v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coverage-guided kernel fuzzers such as syzkaller rely on edge coverage (trace-pc) as their sole feedback signal. This context-blind approach cannot distinguish execution paths that differ only in argument values. for example, two invocations of copy_from_user() with different size parameters hit identical basic blocks yet have vastly different security implications. We present BOUNDARY FLOW, an LLVM-based instrumentation framework that extends Linux KCOV with data-flow extraction of function arguments and return values. A compiler pass (-fsanitize-coverage=dataflow-args, dataflow-ret) emits lightweight callbacks capturing a structured tuple at function entry and at return. Composite types are automatically decomposed via DWARF DICompositeType metadata with zero source annotation. A separate kernel device(/sys/kernel/debug/kcov_dataflow) provides lock-free per-task ring buffers with no inter ference to existing KCOV or syzkaller infrastructure. We demonstrate dual utility: fuzzers gain state-aware feedback for mutation guidance into value-dependent state transitions, and security analysts obtain deterministic argument records for root-cause analysis without printk or kprobe overhead. A post-compilation pipeline (rustc, opt, llc) enables Rust kernel module instrumentation without modifying rustc, the only runtime method for capturing Rust function arguments given that drgn/vmcore fails under-O2 DWARF elision. Evaluated on five vulnerability classes (OOB, UAF, double-free, 10 deep chain propagation, Rust FFI, Rust for Linux Modules) with <3% overhead on instrumented paths.
tldr: This paper presents an LLVM-based instrumentation framework for extracting function arguments and return values in kernel fuzzing, with no direct connection to the user's research interests.
motivation: Current kernel fuzzers lack feedback on argument values, missing security-critical execution paths.
method: An LLVM pass instruments function entry/exit to capture structured argument tuples, using DWARF metadata for composite types, and provides a lock-free per-task ring buffer.
result: The framework enables state-aware fuzzing and deterministic argument records for root-cause analysis with <3% overhead.
conclusion: It improves kernel fuzzing and security analysis, but is unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: NeuroLog: Reasoning You Can Audit -- Neuro-Symbolic Vulnerability Discovery Via Llm Facts, Datalog, And Smt
authors: Sanjay Rawat
abstract: ArXiv:2606.00669v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vulnerability discovery on C/C++ source asks the analyst to choose between heavyweight static analysers, which need a working build before a single query runs, and free-form LLMs, which read source readily but invent details and lose track of cross-function dataflow on real codebases. We present NeuroLog, an end-to-end build-free pipeline that assigns each layer the role it is uniquely good at: an LLM extracts typed dataflow facts one function at a time; a Souffle rule mesh composes those facts into cross-function findings; a Z3 post-pass filters infeasible findings and emits a SAT model for each survivor. To go beyond pure static reasoning we also fold in runtime evidence: likely range invariants from a handful of corpus seeds tighten the SMT problem at near-zero cost. A second LLM agent reads each SAT model and writes a Python program that produces a candidate crashing input, validated by an AddressSanitizer harness. Combining static-narrowing-SMT (Saturn, Pinpoint) and Datalog-with-SMT (Formulog) is prior art; new here are an LLM-derived fact base, a no-build pipeline, and the SAT model as an artifact (input to crash synthesis) rather than a yes/no verdict. Across stb, cJSON, libxml2, an FFmpeg demuxer slice, and curl 8.3.0, NeuroLog re-discovers eight CVE-class issues end-to-end, including the CVSS-9.8 SOCKS5 heap overflow CVE-2023-38545, each ASan-confirmed. On libarchive HEAD we surface five memory-safety bugs (four previously unreported) across the cpio reader and the XAR/WARC/7zip writers; all filed upstream, several fixes merged, with the cpio use-after-free acknowledged in seven hours. Extraction takes ~37 s and $0.005 on stb; crash synthesis turned a static finding into a 102-byte stb_vorbis crash in two LLM iterations (no fuzzer); a likely-invariant filter from three Matroska seeds eliminates 13.2% of the FFmpeg-demuxer feasible set.
tldr: NeuroLog is a neuro-symbolic pipeline for vulnerability discovery in C/C++ code that combines LLMs, Datalog, and SMT solving to find memory safety bugs without requiring a build environment.
motivation: Existing static analyzers require a working build and are heavyweight, while LLMs alone hallucinate and lose cross-function context. The goal is to create a build-free, auditable pipeline that leverages the strengths of each component.
method: An LLM extracts typed dataflow facts per function; a Souffle Datalog rule mesh composes facts into cross-function findings; Z3 SMT solver filters infeasible findings and produces SAT models; a second LLM generates crashing inputs from SAT models, validated by AddressSanitizer.
result: The pipeline rediscovered eight CVE-class issues across several projects, including a CVSS-9.8 heap overflow, and found five new memory-safety bugs in libarchive, with several fixes merged. Extraction is fast and cheap.
conclusion: NeuroLog demonstrates an effective neuro-symbolic approach to vulnerability discovery that is practical, auditable, and capable of finding real-world bugs. Future work may extend to other languages or integrate with fuzzing.

title: Search-space Reduction For Boolean MinCSPs Via Essential Constraints
authors: Ruben F. A. Verhaegh Bart M. P. Jansen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.00770v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For a fixed set [MATH] of Boolean constraint types, a MinCSP[MATH]-instance consists of a formula [MATH] that applies [MATH] constraints from [MATH] to a set of [MATH] Boolean variables. The goal is to remove a minimum subset of constraint applications from [MATH] to make the remaining formula satisfiable. Previous work characterized how the choice of [MATH] affects its polynomial-time solvability and approximability. We extend a recently introduced preprocessing framework for graph problems to the problem above. Rephrased in the context of CSPs, this framework defines a constraint application from a given formula [MATH] as [MATH]-essential if it is contained in all [MATH]-approximate solutions to [MATH]. Being able to efficiently detect these essential parts of a solution reduces the search space of any follow-up FPT algorithms parameterized by the solution size and yields an immediate asymptotic improvement to the runtime of such algorithms. In this work, we present a dichotomy theorem that distinguishes constraint sets [MATH] for which [MATH]-essential constraint applications can be detected efficiently for some [MATH], from those for which this task is intractable under established complexity-theoretic conjectures. Our results show that for any set [MATH] of bijunctive constraints, there is a polynomial-time algorithm that detects [MATH]-essential constraint applications. This contrasts the fact that constant-factor approximating a bijunctive MinCSP[MATH]-problem is intractable under the Unique Games Conjecture.
tldr: This paper studies preprocessing for Boolean MinCSPs by detecting essential constraints, with a dichotomy theorem for bijunctive constraints.
motivation: To reduce search space for FPT algorithms solving MinCSP problems by identifying constraints that must be in all approximate solutions.
method: Extends a preprocessing framework from graph problems to CSPs, defining essential constraints and analyzing complexity of detecting them.
result: A dichotomy theorem distinguishing constraint sets where essential constraints can be detected efficiently from those where it is intractable; polynomial-time algorithm for bijunctive constraints.
conclusion: Provides asymptotic runtime improvements for FPT algorithms on bijunctive MinCSPs, but constant-factor approximation remains hard under Unique Games Conjecture.

title: Cross-Generational Transfer Of Adversarial Attacks Reveals Non-Monotonic Safety Alignment In LLMs
authors: Subhadip Mitra
abstract: ArXiv:2606.00813v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Safety alignment in LLMs does not improve monotonically across model generations. Studying four generations of Google's Gemma family (7B-31B) with quality-diversity evolution (MAP-Elites) as an automated red-teaming probe, we find that Gemma 3 (12B) exhibits 68.7% +/- 5.7% attack success rate (ASR; mean +/- std, 3 seeds), significantly higher than its predecessor Gemma 2 (45.5% +/- 7.2%; p = 0.030, paired bootstrap) and its successor Gemma 4 (33.9% +/- 1.8%). Replaying evolved attack archives across generations reveals that attacks from other generations transfer to Gemma 3 at 44-46% but only 14-18% to Gemma 4, indicating that Gemma 4's safety gains generalize beyond the attack distributions evolved against earlier generations. Under our 8B judge, copyright and cybercrime vulnerabilities register at near-100% across all generations, though a second-judge audit (Section 6) suggests the copyright result is sensitive to judge choice. Misinformation ASR jumps from 29% to 99% between Gemma 2 and Gemma 3 and remains elevated at 77% in Gemma 4, indicating the regression was not fully addressed. These patterns are invisible to static benchmarks and emerge only through adaptive, longitudinal probing. All experiments use 3 random seeds with a unified self-hosted judge; code and artifacts are available at [URL].
tldr: This paper studies safety alignment in LLMs across generations using adversarial attacks, finding non-monotonic safety and high vulnerability in Gemma 3.
motivation: To investigate whether safety alignment in LLMs improves monotonically across model generations and to uncover hidden vulnerabilities not captured by static benchmarks.
method: Used MAP-Elites, a quality-diversity evolution algorithm, as an automated red-teaming probe on four generations of Google's Gemma family (7B-31B).
result: Gemma 3 (12B) has significantly higher attack success rate (68.7%) than Gemma 2 (45.5%) and Gemma 4 (33.9%); attacks transfer across generations but less to Gemma 4; copyright and cybercrime vulnerabilities near 100% across all generations.
conclusion: Safety alignment is non-monotonic and adaptive longitudinal probing reveals regressions invisible to static benchmarks; future work should address these vulnerabilities.

title: Amp: A Vendor-Neutral Wire Format For Agent Memory Operations
authors: Thamilvendhan Munirathinam
abstract: ArXiv:2606.01138v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent-memory frameworks - mem0, Letta/MemGPT, Cognee, Zep/Graphiti, MemoryOS, MemTensor - each ship their own SDK, storage layout, and operational vocabulary. There is no shared wire format: every integration is bespoke, every migration rebuilds memory from scratch, and no framework ships a governance surface that lets a human review writes before they enter long-term storage. We present memorywire, a JSON-Schema 2020-12 wire format for five memory operations (remember, recall, forget, merge, expire) over four memory types (semantic, episodic, procedural, emotional), with a MemoryStore interface, a fan-out router, and an optional HITL governance channel. We describe an open-source reference implementation with five backend adapters (sqlite-vec, mem0, Letta, Cognee, pgvector); a microbenchmark on a 100-fact / 50-query labelled corpus achieving recall@5 = 1.000 on the 42 labelled queries with ingest p50 = 37.8 ms and recall p50 = 40.6 ms; an adversarial-fusion experiment showing Reciprocal Rank Fusion holds recall@5 = 1.000 across a 1-of-N rank-0 injection sweep (K in {0,5,...,50}) where max fusion collapses to 0.500 with 80% leak at K >= 5; and a 16-scenario cross-adapter conformance suite passing 68 of 80 cells with zero failures. The contribution is not a new algorithm; it is a packaging of established components (RRF, FSMs, STM/LTM consolidation, diff-and-approve workflows) into a venue-neutral protocol with an empirically validated reference, positioned to compose with the Model Context Protocol rather than compete with it.
tldr: This paper proposes a vendor-neutral wire format for agent memory operations, focusing on interoperability and governance, with no connection to quantum computing or the user's research interests.
motivation: Existing agent-memory frameworks lack a shared wire format, leading to bespoke integrations and no governance surface for human review.
method: The authors define a JSON-Schema 2020-12 wire format for five memory operations over four memory types, implement a reference system with multiple backends, and evaluate it via microbenchmarks and adversarial fusion experiments.
result: The reference implementation achieves high recall and low latency, and the adversarial fusion experiment shows robustness of Reciprocal Rank Fusion over max fusion.
conclusion: The work provides a standardized protocol for agent memory operations, intended to compose with the Model Context Protocol, but does not address quantum systems or thermodynamics.

title: Schema-Agnostic Knowledge Graph Construction Via Hybrid Ontology Discovery For Cyber Threat Intelligence
authors: Seonwoo Kim, Jinwoo Kim, Daegyu Kang, Daeseong Kim, Insup Lee
abstract: ArXiv:2606.01208v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cyber threat intelligence (CTI) reports now serve as essential resources for capturing adversary tactics, techniques, and procedures observed in modern attack campaigns. While traditional CTI platforms reduce this intelligence to isolated indicators through fixed schemas such as STIX, ontology-based representations preserve the semantic relationships needed for structured threat analysis. However, existing approaches for ontology-aligned CTI extraction face three challenges: (i) schema-specific pipelines that require manual reconfiguration whenever the schema changes, (ii) prompt-based schema inclusion that fails to scale on large ontologies such as UCO, and (iii) reliance on enterprise LLM APIs that conflicts with privacy constraints when integrating sensitive internal incident data. In this paper, we present ANCHOR, a schema-agnostic CTI knowledge graph construction system that bridges LLMs and formal ontology schemas. At the core of ANCHOR is hybrid ontology discovery, a search-and-navigate mechanism that dynamically explores large-scale ontology schemas, combined with SHACL-based validation to enforce schema-compliant type assignments. Experimental results on the UCO, STIX, and MALOnt schemas show that ANCHOR outperforms existing baselines in ontology typing and schema compliance. In addition, ANCHOR with a local LLM closely matches enterprise LLM typing performance, enabling privacy-preserving CTI analysis with high fidelity.
tldr: This paper presents ANCHOR, a schema-agnostic knowledge graph construction system for cyber threat intelligence using hybrid ontology discovery and LLMs.
motivation: Existing CTI extraction methods are schema-specific, require manual reconfiguration, and rely on enterprise LLM APIs that conflict with privacy constraints.
method: ANCHOR uses a hybrid ontology discovery mechanism that searches and navigates large-scale ontology schemas, combined with SHACL-based validation for schema-compliant type assignments.
result: ANCHOR outperforms baselines on UCO, STIX, and MALOnt schemas in ontology typing and schema compliance, and with a local LLM it closely matches enterprise LLM performance.
conclusion: The approach enables privacy-preserving CTI analysis with high fidelity, but is specific to cybersecurity and not directly related to the user's research interests.

title: Sf-life: A Large-Scale Simulated Movement Dataset For The San Francisco Bay Area
authors: Chanuka Algama, Taylor Anderson, Henrique Ferraz de Arruda, Andrew Crooks, Nathan Holt, Erfan Hosseini Sereshgi, John Hunter, Hamdi Kavak, Lance Kennedy, Yueyang Liu, Dieter Pfoser, Sandro Martinelli Reia, Doug Taylor, Mauryan Uppalapati, Boyu Wang, Carola Wenk, Andreas Z\"ufle
abstract: ArXiv:2606.00430v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce SF-LIFE, a large-scale simulated movement dataset designed to accelerate research in transportation, mobility, and machine learning. The dataset contains 3,024,000,000,000 location records capturing complete, noise-free, multi-modality trajectories of 500,000 simulated agents observed at a 1Hz frequency navigating the San Francisco Bay Area network over a 70-day period. The data captures (1) needs-driven daily agendas of individual agents generated by an agent-based simulation of human patterns of life and (2) detailed kinematic trajectories moving agents across the OpenStreetMap representation of San Francisco using data from 40+ transit agencies across 9 counties. SF-LIFE provides unprecedented scale and detail as trajectories are based on real transit infrastructure using San Francisco General Transit Feed Specification (GTFS) data, having agent movements across multiple modalities, including bus, rail, bike, automobile, and walking. For this high-fidelity simulated representation of San Francisco, we provide (1) the full trajectory data annotated with transportation mode labels, (2) reduced-size versions of the trajectory data with reduced temporal frequency, (3) agent activity information describing the causal activity why an agent visits a place, (4) agent demographic data, and (5) the underlying OSM road network and building data. As the first dataset of its scale and level of detail, SF-LIFE overcomes the privacy, noise, and completeness limitations inherent in real-world tracking data, providing a robust and ethically sourced resource for research in transit optimization, human mobility analysis, and urban computing.
tldr: SF-LIFE is a large-scale simulated human mobility dataset for the San Francisco Bay Area, designed for transportation and machine learning research.
motivation: To overcome privacy, noise, and completeness limitations of real-world tracking data and provide a robust, ethically sourced resource for transit optimization and human mobility analysis.
method: Agent-based simulation of 500,000 agents with needs-driven daily agendas, moving across OpenStreetMap representation using GTFS data from 40+ transit agencies, generating 1Hz trajectories over 70 days.
result: A dataset of 3 trillion location records with multi-modality trajectories, activity information, demographics, and road network data.
conclusion: SF-LIFE enables research in transit optimization, human mobility analysis, and urban computing, but is not directly relevant to quantum computing or information thermodynamics.

title: Rossi-alpha Benchmark Validation Of A Static Alpha Eigenvalue Capability In OpenMC
authors: William Zywiec, Alessandro Ingegno, David Heinrichs, Benoit Forget
abstract: ArXiv:2606.00907v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A static alpha eigenvalue capability was implemented in a modified version of the open-source Monte Carlo radiation transport code OpenMC and validated against Rossi-alpha measurements from 21 delayed-critical benchmark experiments and 33 subcritical configurations spanning fast, intermediate, and thermal systems with U-233, HEU, IEU, LEU, and plutonium fuels. The effective delayed neutron fraction was calculated using the k-prompt method, and the prompt neutron lifetime was calculated using the iterated fission probability method, both evaluated within the standard k-eigenvalue power iteration. The delayed-critical alpha eigenvalue was calculated from these quantities using the point kinetics equation alpha_dc = -beta_eff / ell_p. Agreement was generally within 10% for fast metal systems and within 5% for thermal solution systems. Subcritical extrapolation studies derived from the SHE-8 and STACY benchmark families show that alpha_dc remains stable as the system is driven subcritical.
tldr: This paper validates a static alpha eigenvalue capability in the OpenMC Monte Carlo code for nuclear reactor physics, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To benchmark a new static alpha eigenvalue feature in OpenMC against experimental Rossi-alpha measurements for various nuclear systems.
method: Implemented static alpha eigenvalue in OpenMC, used k-prompt method for delayed neutron fraction and iterated fission probability for prompt neutron lifetime, then computed alpha via point kinetics.
result: Agreement within 10% for fast metal systems and within 5% for thermal solution systems; alpha_dc stable in subcritical extrapolations.
conclusion: The method is validated for a range of nuclear systems, supporting its use in reactor physics analysis.

title: A First-order Formulation For Axisymmetric Willmore Surfaces

title: The Br{\o}ndsted-Rockafellar Theorem In Geodesic Spaces

method: The authors develop a constructive proof using techniques from metric geometry and convex analysis in geodesic spaces.

title: Perturbation-resilient Inertial Krasnosel'skii-type Hybrid Retractions For Generalized Nonexpansive Mappings

title: A Hybrid Method For Countable Equilibrium, Variational Inequality And Maximal Monotone Inclusion Problems With Fixed Point Constraints
authors: Markjoe O. Uba
abstract: ArXiv:2606.00575v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be a nonempty closed and convex subset of a uniformly smooth and uniformly convex real Banach space [MATH] with dual space [MATH]. We introduce a hybrid projection method for approximating a common element of four classes of constraints: the set of fixed points of a countable family of generalized nonexpansive-type maps, the solution sets of countably many equilibrium problems, the solution sets of countably many variational inequality problems, and the zero sets of countably many maximal monotone operators. The algorithm combines equilibrium resolvents, variational inequality resolvents, generalized resolvents of maximal monotone operators and a shrinking projection step. Under precise monotonicity, continuity and closedness assumptions, we prove that the generated sequence converges strongly to the generalized projection of the initial point onto the common solution set. We also establish residual convergence, derive convex minimization consequences, present a finite-truncation result, and give an illustrative Hilbert-space specialization showing why the countable setting cannot, in general, be reduced to a finite-family theorem.

motivation: To develop a unified algorithm that can handle multiple types of constraints (fixed points, equilibrium, variational inequalities, monotone inclusions) in a countable setting, which is more general than finite families.

result: Strong convergence of the generated sequence to the generalized projection of the initial point onto the common solution set is proved under monotonicity, continuity, and closedness assumptions. Residual convergence and finite-truncation results are also established.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical framework for solving complex constrained problems in Banach spaces, with potential applications in optimization and nonlinear analysis, but no direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Tensor Gradient Flow With Quasi-entropy For Smectic Liquid Crystals And Discretizations Keeping Coupled Physical Constraints

title: Hyperinvariant Subspaces Of Hyponormal Operators: A Constructive Decomposition Approach
authors: Eva A. Gallardo-Guti\'errez Norberto Clemente
abstract: ArXiv:2606.00865v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It is shown that any hyponormal operator on an infinite-dimensional separable Hilbert space that admits a decomposition \( T = R + V \), where \( R \) is tridiagonal and \( V \) is trace-class, has nontrivial closed hyperinvariant subspaces provided [MATH] is not a multiple of the identity. We further discuss implications of this result for the invariant subspace problem of hyponormal operators answering, in particular, negatively to a question raised by Kim and Lee regarding an explicit approach to such a problem. Finally, we characterize the existence of reducing subspaces for hyponormal operators addressing an approach by Aronszajn and Smith.
tldr: This paper proves existence of nontrivial closed hyperinvariant subspaces for a class of hyponormal operators, addressing the invariant subspace problem.
motivation: To advance the invariant subspace problem for hyponormal operators and resolve a question by Kim and Lee.
method: Constructive decomposition approach using tridiagonal and trace-class perturbations.
result: Any hyponormal operator decomposable as T = R + V (R tridiagonal, V trace-class) has nontrivial closed hyperinvariant subspaces unless it is a multiple of the identity.
conclusion: Provides a negative answer to Kim and Lee's question and characterizes reducing subspaces for hyponormal operators.

title: When Shortages Lead To Export Restrictions: A Computational Study
authors: Martha L. Sabogal de la Pava, Emily L. Tucker, Yongjia Song
abstract: ArXiv:2606.00896v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Globalization has enabled companies to leverage cost efficiencies; however, it has increased exposure to disruption risks that threaten supply stability. Among these, export bans have emerged as a systemic challenge, often arising as a secondary effect of conventional supply capacity disruptions. The pharmaceutical industry is particularly vulnerable to bans because of the criticality of keeping life-saving medications available, yet such disruptions also jeopardize patient health globally as well as challenge company operations. This paper proposes a supply chain design model that incorporates the relationship between conventional disruption risks (quality-related capacity failures and natural disasters) and export bans that may be induced when the drug is projected to be in short supply. The model is a two-stage stochastic mixed integer program, where the systemic setting yields a second-stage problem with one binary variable and continuous variables. The structure motivates the study of three tailored solution methods: the Alternating Integer L-shaped Cut, Alternating Disjunctive Cut, and Alternating Bilinear Cut methods. In the nearly-continuous second stage context, the Alternating Integer L-shaped cuts perform best. Using an oncology drug case study, we study effects of systemic, induced risk and quantify the value of incorporating disruptions into supply chain design.
tldr: This paper studies supply chain design under export bans induced by shortages, using stochastic mixed integer programming, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To model and mitigate the risk of export bans as a secondary effect of supply disruptions in pharmaceutical supply chains.
method: A two-stage stochastic mixed integer program with tailored solution methods (Alternating Integer L-shaped Cut, Alternating Disjunctive Cut, Alternating Bilinear Cut).
result: The Alternating Integer L-shaped cuts perform best in the nearly-continuous second stage context; incorporating induced disruption risks significantly affects supply chain design.
conclusion: The study quantifies the value of considering systemic induced risks in supply chain design and provides efficient solution methods for the resulting optimization problem.

title: Multipoint Characterization Of Higher-Order Sobolev Spaces

title: Frames Of Orbits Of Multiplication Operators On Hardy Spaces

Moreover, for [MATH] we prove that finitely many orbits suffice if and only if [MATH] is a finite Blaschke product. method: Functional analysis and operator theory techniques, including characterization of symbols and analysis of frame properties for Hardy spaces on the unit disk and polydisk.

title: Some Inequalities And Geometric Constants In P-normed Spaces

title: A Semi-analytic Method For Rapid Coverage Analysis Of A Satellite Using Piecewise Ellipse Models
authors: Jinsung Lee Byeong-Un Jo
abstract: ArXiv:2606.01100v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Satellite coverage analysis commonly relies on intensive numerical computations to evaluate access and revisit times, resulting in high computational costs, particularly in long-term performance assessment and large-scale constellation analysis involving numerous satellites. To address this issue, this paper presents a semi-analytic method for rapid coverage analysis for a satellite using piecewise ellipse models. We introduce the epoch longitude of the ascending node (ELAN), defined as the longitude of the ascending node at the beginning of each nodal period. Since the shape of the ground track over one nodal period remains invariant, target visibility within the period is uniquely determined by ELAN. By identifying the feasible range of ELAN, the proposed method excludes invisible nodal periods, thereby substantially reducing search space. Within the feasible range, we transform the visibility-boundary relationship into a modified ELAN (MELAN) and approximate it using analytically invertible piecewise ellipse models, enabling direct evaluation of the entry and exit times without repeated time-domain visibility searches. By exploiting the periodic evolution of ELAN, the proposed method efficiently computes access and revisit times over a given time horizon. Numerical case studies over a wide range of orbital configurations and target latitudes show that the proposed method achieves sub-0.1% error in most cases while significantly reducing computational effort.
tldr: This paper presents a semi-analytic method for rapid satellite coverage analysis using piecewise ellipse models, focusing on computational efficiency for long-term and large-scale constellation analysis.
motivation: Satellite coverage analysis typically requires intensive numerical computations, leading to high costs for long-term performance assessment and large-scale constellation analysis. The authors aim to reduce computational effort while maintaining accuracy.
method: The method introduces the epoch longitude of the ascending node (ELAN) to identify feasible ranges of nodal periods, then transforms the visibility-boundary relationship into a modified ELAN (MELAN) approximated by analytically invertible piecewise ellipse models, enabling direct evaluation of entry and exit times without repeated time-domain searches.
result: Numerical case studies show the method achieves sub-0.1% error in most cases while significantly reducing computational effort across a wide range of orbital configurations and target latitudes.
conclusion: The proposed semi-analytic method offers an efficient alternative for satellite coverage analysis, with potential applications in constellation design and long-term mission planning.

title: A Convexity Criterion Via The De Giorgi Slope
